title: Chapter 52: Lot 41, Part 4 of 5: The Sixth Bell
html:
A man got out of the carriage.
He got out slowly. Carefully. The way a man gets out of a carriage when he is not in a hurry and has never been in a hurry in his life. He put one foot down on the step, and then the other, and then he was standing in the snow by the lych gate, settling his gray cape on his shoulders, and looking up at the church.
Lyra had seen him once before. On Friday night. In her aunt's long room, by the fire, in a chair, tapping on a glass. And at the foot of her aunt's stairs, afterward, with a paper bag of barley sugar in his hand, tapping on the banister. Four. Two. Nine. Three. Tell him I'll see him on Monday.
The Inquisitor.
He was not tall. He was not big. From up here, through a hole the size of a coin in a green glass window, he looked like nobody at all. A slight man of middle height in a gray cape and a plain gray hat. Thin fair hair, going gray, under the hat. A mild, tired face, the face of a country curate who has been up all night with a dying parishioner and is thinking about his breakfast. He did not carry a sword. He did not carry a stick. He had nothing in his hands at all.
He did not look at the young man on the wall. He did not need to. The young man on the wall had gone so still that he might have been part of it.
The Inquisitor came through the lych gate and up the path between the graves.
He walked the way he had got out of the carriage. Slowly. Looking about him. At the yews, with their snow. At the gravestones, leaning, with their names worn away. At a stone angel by the path with no face and one wing broken off. He stopped by the angel for a moment and looked at it, with his head on one side. Then he went on.
At the foot of the three church steps, he stopped.
Silas had not moved. He was still sitting on the top step in the snow with his long legs folded up and his bag beside him and his hands hanging between his knees. He looked down at the Inquisitor at the foot of the steps. The Inquisitor looked up at him.
Lyra could not hear them. She was too high, and the glass was too thick, and the wind had got up and was moaning in the slits of the tower. She could only see.
She saw the Inquisitor take off his hat.
He held it in his hand, against his chest, the way Tibbs had held his hat in the lane that morning. And he said something. Something short. And Silas, on the top step, said something back. Shorter.
And then the Inquisitor came up the three steps, and turned round, and sat down.
On the top step. Beside Silas. In the snow.
Lyra's hands were pressed so hard against the cold stone on either side of the window that her fingers ached through the gloves.
They sat there side by side on the step of Saint Bride's, the tall thin doctor and the slight gray Inquisitor, with the great black door shut behind them and the churchyard in front of them going blue in the dusk. They did not look at each other. They looked out at the graves, both of them, the way two old men look out at a view. Like two men who had known each other for years and had come to sit on a step together at the end of a long day and did not need to say very much.
The Inquisitor put his hand inside his gray cape. Lyra's heart stopped.
He took out a paper bag. A small brown paper bag, twisted at the top. He untwisted it. And held it out to Silas.
Barley sugar.
Silas looked at the bag. For a long time.
Then he shook his head.
The Inquisitor did not seem to mind. He took one out himself, a small amber twist, and unwrapped it, and put it in his mouth. And folded the wrapper. Lyra watched him do it, through the coin-sized hole in the green glass. Folded it in half. And in half again. And again. Small. Smaller. His fingers moving very neatly, very fast, the way her own fingers moved when she folded a letter. Nine times. Ten. Eleven.
Then he put the tiny folded square down on the stone step between them. And left it there.
And then he put his hand flat on the step beside it. And tapped.
Lyra could not hear it. She did not need to. She saw his finger move. Four. A pause. Two. A pause. Nine. A pause.
Three.
Silas did not answer. He did not look at the hand. He went on looking at the graves.
The Inquisitor's hand lay flat on the step for a moment longer. Waiting. Then he took it away. And Lyra thought that he sighed. She could not see it. But his shoulders under the gray cape went down a little, the way shoulders go down when a man lets out a long breath.
And then he lifted his head.
And looked up.
Not at the sky. Not at the roof. At the tower. At the bell chamber, where old Amos was. And then, slowly, down. To the clock room. To the round green window, with its little thick panes of bottle-glass, each with a bubble in it like an eye.
To one pane, near the bottom, with a piece missing.
Lyra did not move. She could not. She had her eye to the gap in the glass and the Inquisitor was looking straight up at it, from the top step of the church, with his mild tired curate's face turned up to the tower in the last of the light, and his pale washed-out eyes, and she knew, quite certainly, the way you know you are about to fall, that he could see her. That he could see her eye at the hole in the glass. That he had known she would be there before he ever got out of his carriage.
He did not do anything.
He did not point. He did not call out. He did not tell the young man on the wall to come and climb the tower. He just looked at her, for a long moment, with no expression on his face at all.
And then he lifted his hat. A little. Just a little. Off his head and back again. The way a man lifts his hat to a lady he knows across a street.
And looked away.
He stood up. Slowly. He brushed the snow off the back of his gray cape with one hand. He put his hat on properly. And he held out his arm to Silas. Not his hand. His arm. Bent at the elbow. The way a man offers his arm to an old friend on an icy path.
Silas looked at it.
Then he got up too. Unfolding himself, all his long legs and arms, the way a heron gets up out of a ditch. He stood on the top step, taller than the Inquisitor by a head. He looked down at him.
And he did not take the arm.
He went down the three steps by himself. And along the path between the graves, by himself, in the snow, tall and thin and black in his too-short coat, with his crooked spectacles, and his long hands at his sides. Past the stone angel with no face. Past the yews. And the Inquisitor walked beside him, a little behind, with his arm still bent, as if he had forgotten to put it down.
At the lych gate, the Inquisitor said something to the young man on the wall.
The young man shut his little black book. He climbed down off the wall. He went to the carriage and got up onto the box beside the driver in the gray cape, and sat there with his book on his knees, and did not look back at the church.
Silas got into the carriage. The Inquisitor got in after him. The door shut.
And the carriage went away along Saint Bride's Lane in the snow, slowly, between the black fronts of the houses, past the lamp at the corner, which somebody had lit now, so that it made a small round yellow light in the blue dusk. And round the corner. And was gone.
Lyra stood at the window for a long time after that.
Then she looked down at the top step. At the place where they had sat.
There was a mark in the snow, where the two of them had been. Two marks, side by side, like the marks two people leave on a bench. And between them, on the stone, a tiny folded square of paper, so small she could hardly see it from up here. A barley sugar wrapper.
And beside it, on the step, where Silas had put it down when he came out of the door, his bag.
His old black doctor's bag, with the brass clasp. Sitting on the top step of Saint Bride's in the snow.
He had left it behind.
Lyra did not remember going down the tower. She remembered afterward that she had counted the steps, all hundred and four of them, out loud, in a whisper, going round and round the stone pillar in the dark with her hand on the rope. She remembered the great west door, and how heavy it was, and how she had to pull it with both hands. She remembered the cold.
She picked up the bag.
It was heavier than she expected. She opened it there, on the step, kneeling in the snow, in the blue dusk, in front of the door with the four nail holes in it. Inside there were no bottles. No instruments. No wet-dog medicine, no knives, no lint, no honey. He had taken all of those out and left them in the crypt.
There was only paper.
A thick bundle of it, tied with tape. Pages and pages, in his long thin sloping hand, the hand of a tired man who wrote fast. A name at the top of each page. Polly. Six. Hook Lane, thought to be. Mother not known. Hums. Kit Flynn. Nine. Holds a spoon. Do not take the spoon. Lisbet Webb. Seven. Tar Street. Cries at the sound of cart wheels. Sing to her. Fifty-one pages. Fifty-one names. How much each one could eat, and how, and when. Which ones had to be turned in the night and which way. Which ones knew their own names, and which ones only knew them sometimes, and which ones did not know them at all.
And on top of the bundle, by itself, a letter. Folded. Sealed with a blob of ordinary candle wax, pressed flat with a thumb.
On the outside, in the same tired hand, it said:
The fifth letter.
To somebody who can read.
Lyra knelt on the step in the snow with the letter in her gloved hands and could not open it. Not yet. She could not see well enough to read. The dusk had got into her eyes.
And on the stone beside her knee, the tiny folded square of the Inquisitor's barley sugar wrapper lay in the snow where he had left it.
She did not pick it up. She did not touch it. She left it there.
Four Who Stay
She read the fifth letter in the long hall, by the braziers, because that was where it belonged.
Corin was still on his bench in the side vault, with Gideon holding his hands and Vespera bent over his face, and could not come. So she stood in the arch of the vault, where he could hear, with the letter in her gloved hands and the lamp held up by Juno beside her, and read it out loud to everybody. To Mrs. Doyle, kneeling by Polly's pallet. To Mrs. Fitch, old and bent, sitting on the end of a pew with her hands in her lap. To the young widow with the baby, whose name was Rose, standing by the nearest brazier with the baby asleep on her shoulder. To Oren on his crate. To Bet, who had come out of the shadows by Ned's vault and was standing very still with her arms wrapped round herself. To Amos, who had come down the crypt steps behind her after the bell and could not hear a word, but stood there anyway, with his old cap in his hands.
And to the children. To the fifty-one. Who could not hear it either, most of them. But she read it to them anyway.
Silas's hand was long and thin and sloping and very fast, and some of the words ran into each other at the ends of the lines where he had not lifted the pen. She read it slowly.
To somebody who can read,
This is the fifth letter. The Inquisitor said I would write one. He was right. He usually is, I'm told.
I have gone to have my little talk with him. Do not come after me. I mean that. Not Vane, not the Captain, not the boy, not any of you. Whatever he wants to know, he can have it out of me, because there is nothing in me now that matters. I have made sure of that. Everything that matters is in this bag.
The pages are the children. One each. Read them. Read them every morning, the way you read Vane his page. Every child's page, every morning, out loud, to the child, whether they can hear it or not. Some of them can hear more than you think. Polly can. Polly could all along. I should have known it sooner.
You will move them tonight. To the house on the Hill. Good. It's the best thing anybody has thought of all winter, and I wish I had thought of it. Move them slowly. Carry them flat. Keep their heads up. Keep them warm. Do not let anybody give them anything sweet to eat, not ever again, not even honey, not for a year. Feed them broth with a spoon, and bread soaked in milk, and talk to them while you do it. Say their names. If you don't know their names, give them one, and say that.
Lyra stopped. She took a breath. Juno, beside her, was holding the lamp very still.
Four of them cannot go.
The long hall was very quiet.
I have known this since Friday. I did not tell Vane, because he had enough to carry. I am telling you now, because now there is nobody else to tell.
Nan Cobb. Five. The pallet under the second pillar on the left.
Little Hob, who has no other name. About three. The pallet by the north brazier.
The Ellery boys. Seven and eight. The two pallets at the far end, together. They hold hands.
They are too far down. They have been falling longer than the others, and faster, and they are nearly at the bottom. If you put them in a cart tonight and take them across the city in the snow and up the Hill, they will die in the cart. I am certain of it. I have seen it happen. Twice this winter. Ned was the second.
If you leave them here, the Health will take them at the seventh bell on Monday.
I have thought about it for two days and I cannot find a third thing. There is no third thing. I am sorry. I am a doctor and I am supposed to be able to find the third thing, and I can't.
So this is what I want. Leave them. Leave them here, warm, by the braziers, with somebody they know. Not alone. They must not wake up alone with men in brown coats standing over them. Somebody must be holding their hands when the carts come. Somebody must be saying their names.
And then, Monday, at noon, a form will come up the pipe to a scribe called Lucian, who copies everything three times. And in the box for the number it will say four. Not fifty-one. Four.
I can live with four. Saints help me, I find I can. I could not have lived with fifty-one.
That is all. Burn this, or don't. It doesn't matter now.
Thank you for reading it. I knew somebody would.
J. Silas. Doctor. Saint Bride's.
Lyra lowered the letter.
Nobody moved.
The braziers ticked. The children breathed. Somewhere at the far end of the long hall, by the last pillar, two small boys lay on two pallets side by side with their hands joined between them on the stone, and did not know that anybody was talking about them.
Lyra found that she could not speak.
She had thought she would argue. She had thought she would say No, the way she had said it to Silas in the arch last night, when he told them about the step. She had thought she would say We'll carry them, we'll find a way, we'll go slower, we'll wrap them in more blankets. She opened her mouth to say it.
And she thought of Ned. Whom she had never met. Who had died on a pallet in this hall on Monday before the sixth bell, while she was in the arches across the river, because he forgot how to swallow. Whose coffin was in the next vault with a tin soldier on it.
I am a doctor, and I am supposed to be able to find the third thing.
She shut her mouth.
It was Mrs. Fitch who spoke.
She was sitting on the end of the pew, old and bent and small, with her black shawl round her shoulders and her hands folded in her lap. She had not said much all week. She never did. She turned the children in the night, slowly, the way Silas had shown her, one after another, all night long, and when they cried she said There in a dry old voice like a door, and that was all. Lyra did not know her first name. Nobody did.
"I'll stop," said Mrs. Fitch.
Everybody looked at her.
"I'll stop with them," she said. "The four." She did not get up. She did not look at anybody. She looked at her own hands in her lap, old and knotted, with the knuckles swollen. "I'm seventy-three. I've buried two husbands and five children and a sister. I've sat with more dying than that doctor has, I shouldn't wonder." Her voice did not change at all. "They won't want me. The men in brown. They don't take old women. Old women aren't worth anything to them." She unfolded her hands. "So I'll sit with them. And hold their hands. And when the carts come I'll say their names. Nan. Hob. The Ellery boys." She paused. "And then the men can take them, and I'll go home."
"Mrs. Fitch—" said Mrs. Doyle, from Polly's pallet.
"Don't, Maggie," said Mrs. Fitch. "I've made my mind up. You go up the Hill with the rest. You're young. You've got arms." She looked up, at last, at Lyra in the arch. Her eyes were small and dark and dry in her old face. "That right, my lady?"
Lyra looked at her.
She wanted to say no. She wanted to say it more than she had wanted to say anything in her life. She wanted to say We'll find a third thing. There's always a third thing. And she knew, standing there with the fifth letter in her hands, that there was not. That Silas had looked for two days, and he was the best of them, and there was not.
"Yes," she said. "That's right."
Mrs. Fitch nodded. Once. As if that settled it.
Then she got up off the end of the pew, slowly, the way old women get up, with one hand on the black oak. And went down the long hall, past the pallets and the braziers and the pillars, to the far end. To the two pallets side by side by the last pillar. And sat down on the cold stone floor between them, with her back against the pillar and her black shawl round her. And took the two small joined hands in both of her own old knotted ones.
And began, very quietly, to say their names.
Lyra folded the fifth letter. She did not burn it. She put it in the list pocket of her mother's gown, with the Lady's list and the lily paper, where Madame Hesper had sewn a pocket for a list. And she went into the side vault, and knelt down beside the bench, and took Corin's gray hands back from Gideon, and held them.
He had heard. She knew he had. His eyes were shut, in his burning red swollen face that was not his face any more. But his finger moved on her palm. Once. And then, after a pause, twice, very quick.
Heard.
One and the double.
"I know," she said. "I know you did."
The Long Carry
They began at the ninth bell, and it took them until the second bell after midnight.
Lyra would remember it afterward in pieces, the way you remember a fever. Not all of it. Not in order. Just pieces, very bright and very sharp, with dark between them.
She remembered the lane behind the church, white with snow, and the four carts waiting in it under no lamp at all. The Duke's second carriage, closed, dark blue, with the gold ship-and-key on the door painted over with soot for the night so that nobody would know it. The Duke's coal wagon, long and black, with high sides and a canvas cover. Two plain farm carts from the Duke's home farm outside the city, flat and broad, with straw on their beds and hoops over them and more canvas. And Abner Cole's coal cart, with the brown mare in the shafts, blowing in the cold, with her blanket on. A. COLE & SON, TALLOW ST. Abner on the seat, black as his cart, saying nothing at all.
And Tibbs on the box of the carriage, with his three-caped coat and his round hat and his walnut face. He saw her come out of Amos's little door with the first child in her arms, and took off his hat, and held it against his chest, and did not put it back on until the last cart had gone.
She remembered the first child. It was Polly. She had wanted it to be Polly. She carried her up the crypt steps herself, through the dark church, past the font and the faded saints, through the passage, into the cold. Polly weighed almost nothing. She was a small bundle of gray blanket and a small gray face with its eyes open, and she lay in Lyra's arms without moving, looking up past her at the sky. And at the door, when the cold air touched her face, she blinked.
Lyra stopped in the doorway and waited.
Polly blinked again. And her eyes moved. Off the sky. Onto the lane. Onto the carts, and the horses, and Tibbs on the box with his hat against his chest. And she looked at them for a long time. And then her eyes came back to Lyra's face, and stayed there.
She did not hum. Not then. But she looked.
Lyra laid her in the Duke's carriage, on the seat, on a folded blanket, with her head on a cushion of blue velvet that smelled faintly of the Duke's lavender water, and tucked the gray blanket round her, and said, "Polly. Your name's Polly. I'll see you on the Hill." And went back down for the next.
She remembered Mrs. Doyle, big and red and cheerful, carrying two at once, one on each arm, like loaves, and singing under her breath the whole way up the steps. The song about the three lamps and the long road. Over and over.
She remembered Rose, the young widow, with her own baby tied to her back in a shawl, carrying a small boy whose name was Tom in her arms in front of her, and stopping at the top of the crypt steps to cry, very quietly, for a moment, and then going on.
She remembered Bet. Ten years old. Who was not sick. Who was the only child in the crypt who could walk on her own and carry. Bet carried Kit Flynn, who was nine and nearly as big as she was. She carried him all the way up, staggering, with his arms round her neck and his wooden spoon held tight in his fist against her back. She would not let anybody help her. At the top she put him down in the straw of the first farm cart, very carefully, and stood there with her chest heaving. And Kit Flynn, in the straw, did not let go of her neck. So she climbed into the cart and lay down beside him, and he held on, and she let him.
"I'll go with him," said Bet. "Ned would have gone with him."
Nobody argued.
She remembered Oren. One arm. Up and down the crypt steps, up and down, a child against his chest in the crook of his good arm each time, and his face dark red with the effort and the cords standing out in his neck. Twenty-two times. She counted. She could not help it. On the twentieth time he stopped at the top of the steps and leaned against the wall with his eyes shut. On the twenty-first he did not stop. On the twenty-second, when there were no more, he stood in the lane by the last cart with his good hand hanging at his side and his sword in its sacking on his back, and said, All's well, my lady, to nobody, and Lyra saw that the hand was shaking.
She remembered Juno, who could not walk, sitting in the straw of the second farm cart at the very back, by the tailboard, with her wrapped feet tucked under her. As each child was laid in the straw she took its hand, and said its name, reading it off Silas's pages by the light of a covered lamp, slowly, letter by letter, the way Lyra had taught her. Lis-bet. Webb. Every one. And then she let go and took the next.
She remembered Gideon, who had not come up. Who had stayed down in the side vault on the floor beside the bench, holding Corin's hands while Vespera finished, because somebody had to and he said he would. And Vespera, at the tenth bell, coming up the crypt steps with soot on her face and blue on her hands and her bundle on her back, and saying, very tired, It's done. It's setting. Don't let him touch it. Don't let him look in anything shiny till the morning.
She remembered Corin. Carried up last but four. By Oren, with one arm, the twenty-third time, when Oren had already said All's well and meant it. Corin lying in the crook of Oren's good arm with his bad leg out stiff in its splints, and his gray hands folded on the Ledger on his chest, and his face.
She did not look at his face. Vespera had said not to look at it too much until it had set. She looked anyway, once, in the light from Abner's covered lamp, as Oren laid him in the back of the coal cart in the straw. And saw a stranger.
A long, sour, narrow face, swollen still and red at the edges, with a gray beard, short and pointed, where Corin had none. A long thin nose with a bump on it. Heavy lids. Deep lines from the nose to the corners of the mouth, down, like brackets. A face that looked as if it had just been told bad news and had expected nothing better.
Fenton.
And then the eyes in it opened, and looked at her. And they were Corin's eyes. Dark and tired and very steady. And the mouth in the sour stranger's face went down at the left corner. Just a little.
She had to look away.
She remembered the four.
She went back down at the end. After the last child was in the last cart and the canvas was down and the horses were stamping in the cold. She went back down the crypt steps by herself, with the covered lamp, into the long hall. It was very quiet now. Very empty. The pallets lay on the floor and in the pews in their rows with no children on them, just gray blankets, rumpled, and the shape of small bodies still pressed into the straw. Forty-seven empty pallets. The braziers were still burning. Somebody had banked them up high, so that they would last the night.
And at the far end of the hall, by the last pillar, in the red light of the north brazier, there were four small shapes still on their pallets. Nan Cobb, under the second pillar. Little Hob, who had no other name, by the north brazier. And the Ellery boys, together, at the far end, with their hands joined between them.
And Mrs. Fitch, sitting on the cold stone floor among them, with her black shawl round her and her back against the pillar. She had moved Nan and Hob. She had moved them herself, slowly, one at a time, so that all four of them were close round her now, like children round a fire. She had one of the Ellery boys' hands in her left hand and Little Hob's in her right, and Nan's head in her lap.
She looked up as Lyra came.
"Go on, my lady," she said. "They're waiting for you."
Lyra stood there with the lamp.
"Mrs. Fitch," she said. "What's your name? Your own name. Nobody knows it."
The old woman looked at her for a moment.
"Hannah," she said. "Hannah Fitch. My mother called me Nan. Like this one." She looked down at the small gray face in her lap. "That's why I took her head."
Lyra knelt down.
She did not know why. She just did. She knelt down on the stone in her mother's gown and put her gloved hand, for a moment, on the old woman's knotted one. On top of Little Hob's small cold fingers.
"Hannah," she said. "Thank you."
"Go on," said Hannah Fitch. "Go on, now. They're cold out there."
And Lyra got up and went. And at the top of the crypt steps, in the dark church, she turned back once and looked down. And saw the red light of the brazier at the far end of the long hall, very small and very far away. And four small shapes. And one old woman in a black shawl, bent over them, with her lips moving.
Then she went out to the carts.
She remembered the ride up the Hill. Not much of it. She rode in the Duke's carriage, with Polly's head in her lap, and three other children on the seats round her, and Rose with her baby and the boy called Tom. The carriage went slowly. Tibbs did not hurry it. Up through the river streets. Over the Tanners' Bridge, where there was a barrier, and a brazier, and a drum boy who stepped out into the road with his hand up. And Tibbs leaned down from the box and said something to him, very low. And the drum boy looked at the carriage, at the door with the soot over the arms. And then he stepped back, and lifted the black and white pole, and let them through without a hook. Lyra never knew what Tibbs said to him. She asked him afterward. He would not tell her.
Up through the Ink Quarter, where the presses were still thudding, even now, at midnight, on Midwinter Eve. Up past the bottom of the Ministry Steps. Up into the wide streets, empty now, with the shop windows dark. And then not up the Crescent but round it, round the back of it, by the Mews Road, a narrow lane behind the great white houses where the stables were and the coach-houses and the dung heaps, and nobody looked out of a window because nobody who lived on the Hill ever looked out of a back window at night.
She remembered the stable gate.
A high wooden gate in a high brick wall at the end of the Mews Road. Old and gray, with iron bands across it, and a wicket door set into it. She knew it. She had gone out through it a hundred times as a child, on her gray pony, with Tibbs walking beside her holding the bridle, to ride in the park. She had never come in through it in the dark.
Tibbs got down off the box with a key in his hand. A small key, brass, on a ring with three others. And unlocked the wicket door. And reached in and drew the bolts on the inside of the big gate, one at the top and one at the bottom. And swung the big gate open, slowly, on its old hinges.
And the carriage went in. And the coal wagon. And the two farm carts, and Abner's coal cart with the brown mare, one after another, into the dark stable yard behind the house on Crown Walk where Lyra Thorne had been born.
Tibbs shut the gate behind them.
And the house stood over them in the dark. Tall and black, with all its shutters closed, and snow on its roof, and no light anywhere.
